en: The *Jiejì* (Sectional Meanings) and Preface to the *Jièzǔ* (Collected Commentaries on the Four Teachings), annotated by Master Yugang, comprises the textual commentary on the *Sìjiàoyí* (Ritual of the Four Teachings). Although it extensively compiles and synthesizes various statements, they are interconnected and mutually illuminating as if completed in a single breath.
The word-by-word explanations and character definitions follow a natural, rhythmic structure, entirely devoid of any visible traces of citation or quotation.
This work, which perfectly emulates Cai Yifeng’s *Iron-Plate Commentary on the Book of Documents*, is truly a great brush of one who has transcended the mundane during the late Ming dynasty.
As for later scholars’ fragmented structural divisions and their various disputations and explanations, they only serve to obscure the original intent;
it is as if the three luminaries are eclipsed within the vast void. Is this not precisely what is meant? It might be better not to use them at all; however, Master Yu follows the text...
Apart from the commentaries, there are what are called "Hand-Eye" (shou-yen) sections; however, the meaning regarding where they agree or differ with other schools does not seem clearly revealed.
I have followed this by providing a topical analysis (*kejie*), naming it "Sections. Why?

It is because I sought only to unravel the gnarled roots and knotted joints of the text, rather than engaging in trivial, fragmented categorization. Furthermore, I studied under my teacher for twenty years and received his transmission eight times.

I have now presented these seven rounds of exposition; at times I have opened the curtains of inquiry to seek instruction, and at others I have sought understanding through the various scriptural divisions.
To share this with my fellow practitioners is merely like adding the light of a torch to the brilliance of the two luminaries.
If future worthies find it unsatisfactory, they need not adopt it. Written on the Mid-Autumn Day of the Wu-wu year at the Ancient Qingliang Temple in Zhejiang by the Bhikṣu Lingyao.

Preface to the *Jie* (Abridged Version) in One Scroll by the Tiantai Bhikṣu Lingyao.

This belongs to the genre of "prefaces" (xu) and "records" (ji), as well as "biographies" (zhuan), which share the same structural principles: first the preface and then the record. To record events is the method of the *Shangshu* and *Chunqiu*. When one wishes to introduce the main text, one first sets forth the causes and conditions; this is done because it would be overly cumbersome to include everything in full. Regarding the *Jiyao* (Essential Records) in three fascicles by the late Master Tian'an Hongji: [The text continues with the formal preface. I have long been aware that the teachings of our school have been transmitted through successive generations, yet their origins and the circumstances of their establishment have remained obscure. Now, having received the *Jiyao* from the hand of the Venerable Master Tian'an Hongji, I have examined it closely. It is a work that clarifies the essential points of the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s profound and subtle intent, and it serves as a guide for those who seek the Way.

Therefore, he does not cite the source in its entirety; those who desire comprehensive detail may consult the *Tianxi Laoren Beijian* (The Elder Tianxi’s Comprehensive Simplification), from which they can learn more.
(Section Four) ... up to the point where it says: "Furthermore, below this, the arising of dharmas is clarified. First, the arising of dharmas through the four conditions is explained.

Regarding the statement that "all other mental factors (*caitta*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and matter (*rūpa*) arise from two conditions," the initial characters [in the original text] are a scribal error.
The phrase "all other" (*śeṣāḥ*) is stated in contrast to "matter" and "non-associated [formations]"; that is to say, it refers to those things which are neither matter nor associated [with mind].
This is similar to the mind. As for the phrase "the remaining conditioned dharmas are inferior," the word "remaining" (*yu*) is a redundant insertion.
(Line seven) The statement that "retribution-born minds and mental factors arise from five causes" below clarifies how dharmas arise from the six causes.

Excluding the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), this is because the retribution-born (*vipākaja*) five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are substantial dharmas (*dravya-dharma*) that have not yet discussed the arising of sharp or dull afflictions (*kleśa*).
Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors arise from three causes. "In the uncontaminated, the upper [stages] lack one" refers to the first fruit (*prathama-phala*).
As for why the uncontaminated requires the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it is like a Bodhisattva with supernormal powers regarding the seven treasures.
Only by attaining the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*) under a tree does one become a Buddha;

because one attains the power of the eight truths, sixteen aspects, eight patiences (*kṣānti*), and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) across the upper and lower stages, one is able to perceive the principle in a single moment. Thus, this requires a collective cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Even if one cultivates the untainted (*anāsrava*), if one encounters adverse conditions, it is difficult to enter the Path; therefore, unimpededness (*anāvaraṇa*) must serve as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It is also by way of conditions.
(Nine lines) The twelve [links] are merely four sets of six.
Below, the explanation clarifies that the twelve are opened up into four sets of six; first, the twelve are correlated with the six causes, and then with the four conditions.

Below, regarding the four conditions: ignorance and formations constitute (1) the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); formations necessarily possess the four characteristics, which constitute (2) the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*);
these four characteristics—namely arising, abiding, change, and cessation—are the "concomitant formations" that produce a common result, constituting (3) the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*);

the summoning of the maturation of consciousness and so forth constitutes (4) the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*); and the pervasive [causes] constitute (5) the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). Among these, [the first] is minimal.

Regarding the first, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*): because within all phenomena (*dharma*) there must necessarily be association between mind and mental factors (*caitta*), it is not established separately.

Just as among the four conditions, [the associated cause] is subsumed within the two types—namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)—so too the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are included therein;
it is likewise unnecessary to establish them separately or to correlate them individually.
(21) In the stage of medium patience (*madhya-kṣānti*), there are thirty-one cycles of reducing the objects of focus (*ālambana*) and the modes of activity (*ākāra*).
The meaning of "reducing the objects" and "reducing the activities" can be understood from the text itself.

Furthermore, the underlying intent of the analysis regarding the reduction of the upper and lower realms is that those of dull faculties in the Lesser Vehicle must first universally contemplate the adverse conditions of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) throughout the three realms.
Having given rise to revulsion, one further contemplates the Path and Cessation, giving birth to a mind of joyful aspiration.
As one fully experiences each of the realms of suffering and pleasure, the feelings of joy and aversion become intimate and direct;

thus one knows that these minds of the thirty-two practices, which take the truth of the principles as their object, are three parts superior to the deluded thoughts and sixfold distractions of ordinary people. Nevertheless, they are still...
The conditioned and outflowing mind is merely used as a means to cease evil and forget [the self];

now that evil delusions have ceased, these conditioned states of mind must also not be retained. Therefore, from this point on, they are gradually diminished until the thirty-first cycle, at which point their reduction is nearly complete;
only the first line of the "Suffering" section remains, and this one must be severed.
In the practice, two moments of mind must be employed: the initial moment of application that severs the object is called "patience" (*kṣānti*);
the subsequent moment, once the severance is complete, is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). This immediately leads one into the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

These two moments correspond to the analysis within the thirty-two aspects of the lower [levels], wherein one contemplates a single practice through these two moments of patience and knowledge. By means of this, one cultivates.
When practicing the abandonment of the delusions below the Four Noble Truths, each instance possesses the two mental states of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) as its cause.
Thus, when the deluded mind is severed one by one upon reaching the Path of Seeing, the two fruits of patience and knowledge are each manifested for every truth of the upper and lower realms.
By inferring the fruit from the cause and verifying the cause from the fruit, one finds that among worldly and world-transcending matters, there has never been a fruit that exists without a cause.
However, during the stage of cultivation, how difficult it is to penetrate the essential knots! When the fruit is finally realized, all things are simultaneously mastered through a single effort;
this is precisely the meaning of sitting for one day at the Nine Days Rapids and thereby crossing all nine rapids.

Furthermore, one should know that although there are thirty-one cycles of the upper and lower stages of Middle Patience involving the reduction of objects and modes of activity, in reality, these reside solely within the Desire Realm.
The internal cultivation within the meditative state of an ordinary person’s body does not mean toiling the body with arduous labor, running up and down in a state of agitation.

(III) Arhats wait for the proper time and the completion of conditions to enter the Path.
The *Great Sūtra Commentary* (Dajinghui shu), in thirty-three fascicles, states: "The assembly of bhikṣus cannot enter nirvāṇa if their conditions are not fulfilled.
For example, when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who requested from Ānanda that four matters be provided."
The Buddha adorned [himself] and commanded Ānanda to prepare [the requisites], whereupon he immediately entered the Path;
this was because a lack of necessities obstructs and distracts the mind, thereby preventing entry.
(The fourth title) As for the remaining three truths, seeing them and subsequently abandoning them through cultivation pertains to those of dull faculties.
In the *Ruxing lu*, the Great Master of Siming answers a Japanese challenge regarding the *Yingluo jing*:

"Śāriputra still regressed and gave rise to great false views while at the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭha-vihāra*); to which teaching does this belong? Is it the sixth stage of the Distinct Teaching? He replies:

"It is indeed the sixth stage of the Distinct Teaching. However, since the first stage of the Distinct Teaching has already severed all views, how could one give rise to them again at the sixth stage?"

Wrong views are like the sands of the Ganges; at the first stage (*bhūmi*), one only severs twenty-eight of the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), while the remaining sixty are severed through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
For those who follow the separate vehicle (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), these views and afflictions are only fully exhausted upon reaching the seventh stage.

Since this [stage] is on the same level as the ultimate fruit of the *piṭaka* and *pāramitā* vehicles, and it is currently only the sixth stage, the afflictions of cultivation are not yet exhausted and wrong views still remain; therefore, even at the sixth stage, there is still the possibility of falling back due to wrong views.
Furthermore, regarding the second fruit, one who has severed the first six of the nine grades of afflictions in the desire realm—

according to the *Lengqie Abatuo Banruo Boluomi Jing*, fascicle three, "Chapter on the Collection of Dharmas"— is explained as being of three different types, with the lowest grade having seven [lifetimes].
Those with middle faculties among those who sever the afflictions of the desire realm attain the fruit after three or five births; those with superior faculties attain it in this very life.
If one has superior faculties, they not only sever the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm but also sever the higher afflictions to attain the fruit of Arhatship.
(The Ten Epithets: "Three births among the devas and two births among humans" means:

one birth among the desire-realm devas where some afflictions are severed; this constitutes one birth, after which one is born once more into the human realm—which is not counted as a separate birth—and then is born again into the heavens to sever further afflictions, which constitutes the second birth, after which one returns to the human realm—which is likewise not counted.
Being born in the heavens and exhausting all afflictions therein is called the "third birth"; this constitutes the inequality among the three types of *kulaṃkula* (house-to-house) practitioners.
As for those who undergo two births: being born in the heavens and exhausting afflictions there counts as one birth;

then, returning once to the human realm does not count as a separate birth; subsequently, being born again in the heavens and exhausting all afflictions there is called the "second birth," which constitutes the inequality among the two types of heavenly *kulaṃkula*.

Regarding the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner: there are three births as a family-to-family practitioner together with human births, totaling five births; or two births as a family-to-family practitioner together with human births, totaling three births.
(Eleventh Title) They are endowed with nine types of faculties.

There are four types of *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family): those who are equal among gods but unequal among families, those who are equal among families but unequal among gods, those who are equal among both gods and families, and those who are unequal among both gods and families.
These four positions, together with the five subsequent [types], constitute the nine kinds of *kulaṃkula*.
Although the name "one who goes from family to family" is one, there are clearly four different types based on the relative numbers of gods and human rebirths.
(14) Seven types of parinirvāṇa.

In the thirty-third fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Kāśyapa-parivarta explains the listing of seven individuals from the Ganges as follows: first, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*);

second, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon taking birth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*); third, one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*); fourth, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*); fifth, one who flows upward (*ūrdhvasrotasparinirvāyin*); sixth, one who attains parinirvāṇa in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyin*).

The seven types of *ārūpya-samāpatti* (attainments of the formless realm) are listed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in agreement with the Great Sūtras, because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* constitutes the skeletal core of a single school’s doctrine.
(Fifteen: Diagram of the eighteen heavens of the form realm for total transcendence.)
The thirty-third fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that within the fourth dhyāna there are again two kinds of samādhis:

those who delight in the bliss of entering the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and those who delight in wisdom and enter the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). There are five stages of distinction, namely:
inferior, middling, superior, most excellent, and supreme. One cultivates these five types of "interlaced perfuming" (*miśra-bhāvanā*) dhyānas by interposing one [moment] between two non-full minds.
When a tainted mind perfumes this single moment of a tainted mind, it also becomes untainted;
together with the fifteen untainted minds that are thus formed, one completes the square and circle of the Akaniṣṭha dhyāna.

(No. 20) There are many distinct designations for Arhats.

This is because, at the very outset while on the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they gave rise to the resolve for awakening and cultivated their faculties (*indriya*) in a thousand different ways;

consequently, after the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), there are nine distinct lineages of faculties that bypass the intermediate stages, and after the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), there are twelve thousand nine hundred.

Among the one hundred and sixty types of *āsravakṣaya* (exhaustion of outflows), up to the stage of the fourth fruit (*phala*), there are naturally two, three, six, and nine distinctions regarding the nature of the fruit of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning),

(Three lines) Those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) enter directly by taking emptiness as their object.

Question: If a person of wisdom directly enters [the path] by taking emptiness as their object, for what reason do they further practice meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) such as the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*)?

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these nine perceptions are the contemplation for attaining liberation; by taking the nine impure contemplations as the object, one opens up the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*);

by taking the four foundations of mindfulness as the object, one opens up the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad bodhipakṣadharmāḥ*); and by taking the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as the object, one opens up *nirvāṇa*.
As for the gate, they are still those who have attained liberation through wisdom by directly entering via principle (the twenty-fifth category, the ten practices).
Fourth, there is retrogression from the spiritual lineage; fifth, there is no retrogression from the fruit that was not previously attained.

The two characters "non-original" (非先) serve as a general summary of the two types of regression previously mentioned: regression from the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and regression from the fruit (*phala*).

Regarding these four [types of regression], regression from the lineage occurs only after one has entered a refined root-lineage (*indriya-gotra*); there is no regression from a lineage that was not originally so.
Likewise, regression from the fruit occurs only after one has entered a refined fruit; there is no regression from a fruit that was not originally so. This is not...
Above the first two characters, the character "first" (先) should be added; only then will the meaning become clear.

For example, if one explains "first" and "not-first" in terms of *gotra* (nature), then the "first nature" is non-retrogressive, whereas the "non-first seed-nature" (*bīja-gotra*) that has entered through cultivation is subject to retrogression.

The preceding text is a restatement of the meaning of the first two lines; the four lines following "knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows" (kṣayajñāna) constitute the formal verse of the treatise.

Or, it may be that which was originally abandoned; such a person, relying on the first basis, abandons the [defilements] of the upper eight stages through contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*), and upon reaching the fulfillment of the sixteenth moment of mind, they immediately leap to the state of one beyond training.

If one enters by means of both the path of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the path of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), as is the case for those within the inner disciples, then because these two paths are firm and without regression, they are steadfast.

both parts clarify the reason why those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) may fall away, and thus they must not be separated.

The reason why the Arhat of Right Discrimination (samyak-pravicaya) is immovable and non-retrogressive is precisely because the meaning of the five types of retrogression has already been explained and clarified previously;

therefore, we now distinguish the meaning of the sixth type, which is non-retrogressive. Question: It was stated previously that those liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) are subject to retrogression.
Since the Immovable One is also a person liberated by wisdom, it would follow that the Immovable One should likewise be subject to retrogression.

Question: For what reason do those who have cultivated their nature not both fall back? Answer: Among the first five types, how could those liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) ever necessarily fall back?
It is only when their tainted knowledge (sāsrava-jñāna) encounters adverse conditions that one speaks of falling back from the fruit.

If even those of the five stages who possess untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) do not fall back, how could it be said that those with immovable wisdom (akopya-dharma) fall back? This is the refutation.
This passage concerns the immovability and non-retrogression of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that when discussing in general whether those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) may regress, the point is to demonstrate that if, while still on the path of causes, one relies upon a mind that is tainted (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then even a minute deviation will result in a lack of firmness at the stage of fruition;

thus, even though they have reached the state of no-more-learning, they might still be unable to avoid regression despite being in, abiding in, or guarding [the fruit]. How much more so for those still in training (*śaikṣa*)?

If one falls into such a state as the ruin of Zhengdai, as previously mentioned regarding the incident of "preparing tadpoles with a frog," then the warning that "treading on frost leads to hard ice" applies;
those who resolve their minds must be careful from the very beginning.

3, Section 3), how could the phrase "reuniting the two and returning to the Āgamas" mean that Kātyāyanīputra and others are the persons who reject [the teaching], while the phrase "reuniting the two" refers to the provisional [teachings] that are rejected? How could it be so?

One should know that the Dharma was taught provisionally at the Deer Park; therefore, while there were those like the Water-Buffalo Bodhisattvas who had not yet severed their delusions, now, through the Vaipulya [sūtras] such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they have become followers of the Mahāyāna.
How much more so, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has revealed and clarified that everything is nothing other than the white ox on the open ground.
How can you still cling to the provisional teachings of the twelve years prior to compose a treatise to clarify the meaning of "A"?
If it were the case that there must be bodhisattvas who have not yet severed their delusions, then after the revelation and manifestation [of the truth] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
they would still be the same as they were during the twelve years prior.

Because eight numbers have been omitted therein, it refers to sixty *asaṃkhyeyas* as being fifty-two numbers;
however, the term *saṃkhyā* (number) refers to that which is counted when time is immeasurable.

(Sixth Section, Line 15). From the passage "From this point on, one shall forever be free from the female body" onwards...

(Section 11, Line 7) Regarding "Qu-pin divided Jambudvīpa into seven parts to cease strife":
In the fifth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is stated that Śākyamuni was formerly the son of the minister of King Maitreya, named Mahāgovinda.
When he succeeded his father as regent, there were six Kṣatriya kings; Govinda divided [Jambudvīpa] for them.
He divided the waters and lands of Jambudvīpa into seven portions and bestowed them upon six Kṣatriyas and the Great King as seven great kingdoms.
Later, he conversed with a Brahmā youth; because the youth loathed his body’s odor, he subsequently left the household life to practice the Way and was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The statement in the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) that "dependent origination is itself emptiness" reflects the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*;
the statement regarding the four noble truths of non-arising reflects the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Since none of the Four Teachings fail to first present this fundamental principle, we know that the initial listing of the *Āgama* and *Candrapradīpa* sūtras—while possessing names—lacks substance, as they are not the primary texts relied upon.

In the fifty-seventh chapter, "The Profound Lamp-Torch," of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), which explains the stages of practice common to both [the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva vehicles],
it elucidates in detail the characteristics of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

In response to the question of why views are abandoned together in the third and fourth stages: this statement merely uses the specific to clarify the general meaning.

While the specific sense of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is predominant in the discussion of the third and fourth stages, the general sense of "view" is secondary. Furthermore, regarding "not emerging from absorption," the specific [meaning] is distinct.

Although it is said that the afflictions are severed at the first stage (*bhūmi*) by borrowing a specific name for a general category, this merely establishes the intent of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

One must understand that from the third to the fourth stages, one does not emerge from contemplation; these three stages constitute the severing of the views of the "prior" [path], while the fourth constitutes the severing of the views of the "subsequent" [path], much like the two moments of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) in the Treasury Teaching (*piṭaka-śāsana*).
Moreover, the three characters "not emerging from contemplation" (*ch'u pu ch'u kuan*) are entirely beyond the realm of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
The true meaning of this matter clearly demonstrates that the practitioner of contemplation suddenly severs the eighty-eight *āsravas* within a single *kṣaṇa*.

This is because the capacities of those in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) are mixed, and the principles of the distinct stages (*bhūmi*) are predominant; thus, it is said to be the third or fourth stage.

In reality, however, it is like the final moment of the "World-First" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), which introduces one into the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) in a single *kṣaṇa*, and is therefore termed "not departing from contemplation."

just as the wick is not burned by the initial moment of fire, nor is it burned by the final moment of fire, so too [is the attainment of enlightenment]. Furthermore, [the text] explains...
The ten stages of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
Regarding the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,

the fourth fascicle clarifies that entering the "mind-made body of the bliss of samādhi" represents the meaning of the true emptiness of the Shared Teaching, while entering the [fifth stage] represents the distinct teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).

Abiding in the realization of the self-nature of dharmas, the manifestation of the mind-made body (manomayakāya) that establishes the Buddha-dharma is the meaning of the Separate Teaching’s emergence into the provisional;

entering the ten stages of practice (bhūmi), the manifestation of the innate, effortless mind-made body is the meaning of the Perfect Middle Way’s entry into the ten stages of dedication (pariṇāmanā).
(Section 31, Line 12) The three roots explain the source.
For example, the single phrase "neither outflowing nor non-outflowing" is fundamentally pervasive of the True [Middle], yet there are two interpretations—distinct and non-distinct—which differ;
